question: What is the meaning of updates in relation to history?
description: Updates in relation to history refer to changes made to the maintenance information in the digital product passport (DPP) during the product use phase by third-party service providers. These updates are crucial for consumers because maintenance or repair services can often alter the quality and components of a product. The proposed framework enables the updating of maintenance history, such as condition-based maintenance/repair, by third-party service providers. This information is important for recyclers/manufacturers to understand recycling or circularity potential and support decisions making at the end of life of a product.

3.3.2. Scenario to illustrate the process of enabling information update by a
3rd party service provider during product use phase
This framework can help to enhance data completeness by enabling
3rd party services such as repairers and maintenance professionals to
update the information during the use phase. This is a requirement from
ESPR which is missing in all the current DPP designs. Updating the
service log during the use phase is not included in current DPPs, yet this
is important for consumers because maintenance or repair service
changes may often change the quality and components of the product.
To illustrate the application of our proposed framework, a scenario is
outlined here. Fig. 9 describes the step-by-step workflow of user verifi-
cation for data updates in the service log. The user (a service provider)
can scan the QR code of the EV battery using a product tag scanning App
to get access to the relevant product data in the battery DPP as shown in
steps 1 and 2. The user can choose to view the relevant technical data or
update it as shown in step 3.
To view or update information, the service provider (e.g., repairers,
maintenance professionals) need to prove that they are who they claim
to be (i.e., verification of their identity) and are authorised to perform
the action defined in the DPP access rights and permissions (i.e., what
data the service providers is allowed to access and update). The user’s
identity is then verified using local standard mechanisms such as Cer-
tificate Authorities (CAs) and Membership Service Provider (MSP). An
MSP can be an authorised local identity registry to verify the service
provider. For example, in Norway, the organisation number of a com-
pany/organisation can be looked up and verified using the official reg-
istry (e.g. The Brønnøysund Register Centre). For this case, in Step 4 of
Fig. 9, the service provider provides their 9-digit organisation number
and their email as shown on the left screen in Fig. 10 (left). A smart
contract has a list of authorised service providers for the product. In step
5, a smart contract will verify the user ID with the official registry to
ensure that the organisation is registered and is a legal entity for the
intended role. Afterwards, the smart contract will authenticate the user
using the user organisation’s authentication services and the provided
user credentials. Once verified, the service provider can update the
maintenance information in Step 6, as shown in Fig. 6 (right).
3.3.3. Theoretical implication
Digital solution components, such as the use of blockchain technol-
ogy with smart contracts to verify user identities and control access
rights, have significantly enhanced security at the digital layer. How-
ever, challenges remain in addressing security concerns related to the
transition from physical to digital realms, including risks associated
physical tampering (Jiang et al., 2022). As data carriers serve as the
initial point of access for customers, security measures for this first line
of defence must also be considered. QR codes, commonly used in

Updating the service log during the use phase is mentioned in current
DPPs. According to ESPR, DPPs should not only provide accurate,
complete, and up-to-date information but also enable the updating of
data. From Table 1, we found limited studies focusing on how to ensure
that maintenance history is properly recorded and how this interaction
should be designed to ensure that maintenance history remains up-to-
date during the maintenance phase by third-party service providers.
For instance, Plociennik et al. (2022) and Munaro et al. (2019) high-
lighted the need for information generated during the product use phase
to be stored in DPPs, but the details on how such data can be included
are not provided. This is crucial for consumers because maintenance or
repair services can often alter the quality and components of a product.
3.3. Proposed framework to enable dynamic information flow
The literature review indicates that current DPP development lacks
focus on updating information during the maintenance phase by third-
party service providers. To address this gap, we propose a blockchain-
based DPP system design that facilitates dynamic information flow
and ensures secure and effective updates, particularly for maintenance
information provided by third-party service providers during the prod-
uct use phase. Given the limited emphasis in the literature on post-
launch data inclusion mechanisms, our proposal highlights the impor-
tance of incorporating user verification and authorization within the
blockchain-based DPP system.
Based on the findings in Section 4, the core requirements for this
framework include data source, data carrier, data security, and user
access and verification. Since the data source involves third-party ser-
vice providers, a blockchain-based DPP is suitable to enhance data se-
curity and trust in data sharing, as it has been widely adopted in DPP
initiatives. Smart contracts can be used to verify the identity of service

3.3.1. Framework explanation
To address the data collection of maintenance service by 3rd party
service provider during the launch of the product of DPP, we proposed
conceptual framework consists of several key components such as the
DPP and user management illustrated in. Our framework enables the
updating of maintenance history (e.g. condition-based maintenance/
repair) by 3rd party service provider. This information is important for
recyclers/manufacturers to understand recycling or circularity potential
and support decisions making at the end of life of a product.
The DPP should use a unique identifier so that all data generated
throughout the product life cycle can be associated with it. ID man-
agement is a central aspect of DPP management. When a DPP is created,
a unique ID (e.g., a URL) will be assigned to the DPP to ensure that the
DPP can be updated and accessible throughout all the product life cycle
phases. We propose the use of standards, such as GS-1 Digital Link (GS1,
2023), to ensure globally identifiable, unique IDs. This is crucial for data
consistency in a decentralized system. In addition, a product tag that
contains a data carrier such as QR codes or RFIDs will be used to link
physical products with their DPPs. A scanning app (e.g., a mobile QR
code reader) can then be used to retrieve and update the DPP data.
A key component in our framework is the role of blockchain tech-
nology. Blockchain can provide an immutable record of events, ensuring
that every update, transaction, or change is recorded in chronological
order. This not only enhances the reliability of the information within
the DPP but also builds trust among all stakeholders involved.
